definition.text: Mangrove forests are a form of natural capital that yields many goods and services to coasts, local communities and society at large.

facts.text: Some mangrove outputs, such as timber, are traded in ordinary markets, where their value shows up as a price.
Mangroves give nursery habitat to many species, including commercial fish and crustaceans, helping keep local fish and shellfish numbers up.
An estimated 75 percent of the prawns and fish caught commercially in Queensland, Australia, depend on mangroves for part of their life cycle.
Mangroves help keep water clean by cycling nutrients, and they slow water so sediment settles out.
Mangrove forests take carbon from the air and store it in their biomass and waterlogged soils, adding to coastal blue carbon stocks.
At least 35 percent of the world's mangroves were destroyed in a single decade, faster than tropical rainforests disappeared.
Economic arguments weigh most in mangrove conservation, yet the true economic value of mangroves is hard to measure and key ecological functions are undervalued.

title: Mangroves as coastal protection
article: Ecological values of mangroves#Endangered mangrove coastlines and human development

definition.text: Mangroves shield shorelines in storms because their tangled roots absorb wave energy and slow the water passing through.

facts.text: Wave energy may fall by 75 per cent as a wave passes through 200 meters of mangrove forest.
Shorelines covered by mangroves erode less, or much more slowly, than bare shorelines when waves are strong.
Keeping a healthy mangrove forest is cheaper than seawalls, which can increase erosion in front of the wall and on neighbouring land.

title: Mangrove water filtration
article: Ecological values of mangroves#Improving coastal water quality

definition.text: Mangroves keep coastal water clean by trapping, removing and recycling nutrients, pollutants and particles from land before they reach reefs and seagrass.

facts.text: Mangrove roots slow the water so sediment settles, and toxins and nutrients bound to the sediment are removed with it.
Because building a wastewater treatment plant is costly, mangroves are often chosen to receive effluent, and purpose-built mangrove wetlands now treat sewage and aquaculture waste.
Runoff is filtered first by coastal forests, then mangroves, then seagrass beds before reaching coral reefs, which need these buffers to avoid algal overgrowth.

definition.text: A nutrient cycle is the movement of living and non-living matter back into the making of new living matter: nature's recycling system.

facts.text: Energy flows one way through an ecosystem and is not reused, while mineral nutrients move in cycles.
The cycles include the carbon, sulfur, nitrogen, water, phosphorus and oxygen cycles, among others.
Recycling in nature is controlled largely by decomposition, and food webs full of different species do the work.
Natural recycling is one of the ecosystem services that sustain human well-being.
Some ecosystems run a nutrient debt and act as sinks while others have a surplus and act as sources, depending on climate, landform and geology.
Most textbooks treat 'nutrient cycle' and 'biogeochemical cycle' as the same, though 'nutrient cycle' usually means cycling within one ecosystem.
In 1749 Carl Linnaeus described nature's recycling in his book Oeconomia Naturae, the 'economy of nature'.

title: Complete recycling debate

definition.text: A dispute over whether matter can be recycled completely, with 100% of waste rebuilt into new material without end.

facts.text: Howard T. Odum held that living systems can gather chemical elements without limit as long as energy, such as sunlight, is available.
In 1979 Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen proposed a 'fourth law' of entropy saying complete recycling is impossible.
The fourth law has been rejected in light of observed ecological recycling, though some authors say complete recycling is impossible for technological waste.

contested_note: Georgescu-Roegen said complete recycling is impossible; others reject this for ecosystems but some accept it for technological waste.

definition.text: An ecosystem engineer is an organism whose actions leave a lasting change in its surroundings, also called niche construction.

facts.text: Ecosystem engineers can change how efficiently nutrients are recycled.
Earthworms churn the soil as they move and feed, carrying nutrients down into the mineral layers.
Worm castings hold undigested material that bacteria and other decomposers can then break down.

definition.text: Recycling in human industry differs from recycling in ecosystems in scale, complexity and organization.

facts.text: Industrial recycling relies on people and technology rather than food webs to turn waste back into marketable goods.
Only 7% of all plastic waste is recycled by industry; the other 93% is presumably absorbed by natural recycling systems.
Many human 'technoecosystems' compete with or feed off natural ecosystems.
